doc.title: Mike Longo interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2019

title: Dizzy's coaching, touch, African drumming and the metronome
summary: Dizzy patiently taught Longo through touch and rhythm; Longo criticizes jazz education for leaving out African drumming and teaching the metronome.

story.theme_name: Teaching jazz: schools, students and advice to the young
story.community_name: What to think while improvising: wrong notes and being in the moment

blocks.x: Did you ever try doing something on a gig that he didn’t like and that he told you?
Yeah. As far as your playing I guess.

Well man when I was first was with him I used to tell the cats that if I was Dizzy I would have fired me. But he kept saying, “I know it’s coming, I know it’s coming.” And he was very patient with me. And so there would be times where I’d be playing and he’d come over and sing something in my ear and next thing you know I’d go how am I doing this? Or he’d play the tambourine in my ear. Or he would play something on his horn that would make me play a certain thing and then I would be in a different place. And a big part of that is your touch. There’s a certain touch involved in jazz and this is what is eluding jazz education today, they’re leaving all that out. They don’t know that exists.

It’s on my DVD series. But if you’re playing African drumming, and also there’s these catalystic type melodic exercises that Dizzy showed me. So you have to learn, you see the difference is there’s something, jazz is polymetric whereas classical music is monometric and monorhythmic. But when you’re playing jazz man, you’re in 4/4, 3/4, 6/8, 5/8 and all different tempos all meshing together at the same time. And so when you are able to play that on a drum, when you go to the piano your touch has got all that in it, that’s on a saxophone, on a bass, all that. And so Oscar used to call it touch, time, tone, technique and taste. And so it’s not just any touch. You can’t play jazz like you play Mozart, with that kind of touch. And so what’s happening in jazz education now is they’re leaving out the African part of jazz, which in my estimation is criminal. Because that’s the essence of jazz. And so they’re teaching everybody what to play instead of how to play. And that’s a big problem. It’s not their fault, they don’t know any better. © Fillius Jazz Archive -13-

Jazz education has been around long enough now that it seems to me a lot of the professors were taught by other jazz professors, who were taught by other jazz professors, and they, a lot of them haven’t really played in real life.

They haven’t played with anybody. Yeah. Well there’s two ways to learn. You can learn like when I first played with Cannonball — I played with Cannonball and the next thing you know I’m playing stuff I don’t understand — because he would pull me in with his playing. I’m comping behind him. And next thing you know the piano is feeling different and I’m playing all this stuff and it’s coming out in my touch. And so that was what they used to call apprenticeship through osmosis. But with Dizzy I actually learned the principles behind it and that’s what I put in the DVD series.

And I teach people how to play the African drumming and then how to put it on the instrument. And so when you learn this drumming thing, this is an oversimplification, but jazz is basically African drumming on a piano. And so you hear guys talking about, “Well they’re just subdividing” or they’re talking about practicing with a metronome. So I told this guy, I was having this big argument on the internet with this Ph.D. from North Carolina. And he took issue with me telling people don’t practice with a metronome. So I said, “Man, listen to a drum section from Ghana. The time is perfect. The depth of swing, the depth of tone is all perfect. When they get finished playing, go ask how many of you guys practice with a metronome. And how many of you guys know what subdividing means. So apparently they’re doing something else.” So I just say, “You better find out what that something else is,” instead of teaching all that stuff they’re teaching in the school. It’s not their fault man, they don’t have the information. But this stuff like playing with a metronome on two and four and practicing. That’s the worst thing you could do in life. I’ve played with Elvin, I’ve played with all those drummers man, they don’t feel like a metronome. A metronome is, first of all, the reason they call it a pulse, if you feel here, that’s the way you keep time in jazz. Now you say, who invented the metronome? Man did. Who invented this? You dig?
And when I say there’s a depth in jazz in Dizzy’s music, it comes from this.
